title: Digitalization and Procedural Formalization of Bill of Export
summary: The Bill of Export has evolved from a purely manual, paper-based declaration to a hybrid system that mandates electronic submission via the Customs Computerized System. Over time, the policy has shifted to integrate this document into broader digital audit trails, including EGM synchronization and post-clearance audit requirements.

evolution.submission_method: Transitioned from manual-only to mandatory electronic submission with paper-based backup requirements.
evolution.institutional_role: Shifted from a simple clearance document to a critical audit instrument for post-clearance verification and AEO compliance.

timeline.change: Formalized the requirement for Customs Agents to submit Bills of Export via electronic or manual methods.
Mandated the synchronization of Bill of Export with EGM and established it as a core document for post-clearance audit.
Expanded the role of the Bill of Export to facilitate self-inspection and duty payment processes for AEO-certified entities.

Customs Agent: A Customs Agent is required to perform various professional duties, including representing clients, verifying documents, and ensuring regulatory compliance during import and export processes.

The agent must ensure that all funds received from clients for government dues are deposited promptly into the public treasury and that funds received from the government on behalf of clients are paid to them without delay.
Customs Agents are prohibited from exerting undue influence on customs officials, borrowing money from customs staff, or acting as a guarantor for loans taken by such officials.

The agent must maintain all records, financial documents, bills, and correspondence related to licensing for a minimum period of three years in their office and present them to the customs authority upon request.

Agents are responsible for providing accurate information to clients, notifying customs authorities of any discovered false documentation, and cooperating fully with the customs authorities in the execution of their duties.
Bill of Entry: A Bill of Entry must be submitted electronically or manually, along with appropriate valuation forms, by the Customs Agent after verifying all relevant import documents.
Bill of Export: A Bill of Export must be submitted by the Customs Agent to the customs authority, ensuring that the process remains transparent and that the document is not held in the agent's possession after the customs procedure is completed.
Valuation Rules 2000: Customs Agents must ensure that all declarations for the determination of imported goods' value are prepared and submitted in accordance with the provisions of these rules.
Customs Station: Customs Agents are prohibited from collecting any data or records belonging to the customs authority at a customs station without receiving prior permission from the relevant authorities.
Customs Licensing Authority: The Customs Agent must notify the licensing authority in writing immediately upon any change of their business address.

Customs Agent: A Customs Agent is required to submit their authorization letter from the client to the relevant customs authority.
They must verify client documents, prepare and submit accurate Bills of Entry or Bills of Export, and ensure all required customs declaration forms are filed according to the Valuation Rules.
Customs Agents are obligated to notify customs authorities in writing if they discover that a client has provided false information or failed to comply with the law.
They must collect government dues from clients and deposit them into the state treasury promptly, and conversely, pass on any refunds received from the government to the client without delay.

Customs Agents are prohibited from exerting undue influence on customs officials, accessing customs records without permission, employing individuals whose licenses were previously rejected or cancelled, or engaging in financial transactions like lending money to customs officials.
They must maintain all transaction records, bills, and correspondence for a minimum period of three years and ensure these records are made available to customs officers upon request.

Customs Agents are responsible for maintaining a professional standard of knowledge, skill, and integrity while providing maximum cooperation to the customs authorities in the discharge of their duties.
Bill of Entry: Customs Agents must submit the Bill of Entry via electronic or manual methods, as applicable, accompanied by all necessary supporting documentation and valuation declarations.
Bill of Export: Customs Agents must submit the Bill of Export via electronic or manual methods, as applicable, accompanied by all necessary supporting documentation.
Customs Valuation (Determination of Valu: The declaration of value for customs purposes must be carried out in accordance with the provisions specified in these rules.
Customs Authority: Customs authorities have the right to request documents from a Customs Agent, and agents are prohibited from concealing, removing, or destroying such requested records.

Export General Manifest: Following shipment, an export general manifest generated by the customs computerized system must be maintained by the exporting entity for audit purposes.
Bill of Export: A copy of the bill of export must be preserved alongside other export documentation to facilitate future customs audits.
Deemed Export: Deemed exporters must issue Value Added Tax invoices for supplied goods, ensuring that specific details such as utilization permission numbers, back-to-back letter of credit numbers, and direct exporter information are accurately recorded on the invoice.
Value Added Tax Invoice: All Value Added Tax invoices and supporting export documentation must be retained by the relevant entity for the purpose of subsequent audit inspections.
Export Proceeds Repatriation: Entities are required to provide proof of export proceeds repatriation, including copies of foreign demand drafts and proceeds realization certificates, during the course of an audit.

Customs Act 1969: Section 146 of the Act is maintained as the primary legal framework, with these provisions ensuring that export procedures do not undermine existing statutory requirements.
Export Customs Clearance: Exporters are required to submit an export declaration, such as a bill of export or shipping bill, through the customs computerised system upon arrival of goods at the customs house or station.
Appropriate customs officers must verify the submitted documents for accuracy and completeness before completing the customs clearance process for export consignments.

Customs authorities reserve the right to physically inspect export consignments before shipment, and any discovered discrepancies between the declaration and the physical goods must be resolved according to legal procedures.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is responsible for prescribing the official format and procedures for generating export manifests within the customs computerised system once shipment is complete.
Proceeds Realization Certificate: The lien bank of an exporting institution must issue this certificate as proof that the total export proceeds have been repatriated to Bangladesh within the prescribed timeframe or any extended period granted by the central bank.
Commissioner of Customs: If export proceeds are not repatriated within the allowed time limits, the Commissioner of Customs or an authorized delegate is empowered to demand an amount equivalent to the export value from the exporter in Bangladeshi currency, including applicable interest.
Export Manifest: An export manifest must be generated within the customs computerised system in a prescribed format after the export consignment has been shipped.
The export manifest number must be referenced alongside the bill of export number in the import-export statements prepared by industrial institutions for audit purposes.

Customs Computerised System: The system serves as an electronic medium for the submission of the Bill of Export by registered users.

Customs Duty: Payment of all duties payable on the goods is a mandatory prerequisite for export clearance.
Exporter: Exporters are obligated to fulfill any conditions, guarantees, or undertakings imposed upon them and must provide proof of export proceeds or other acceptable documentation to the customs officer.

(২) যে উদ্দেশ্যে নমুনা গ্রহণ করা হইয়াছিল তাহা সম্পন্ন হওয়ার পর উক্ত নমুনা, যদি সম্ভবপর হয়, মালিকের নিকট ফেরত দেওয়া হইবে, কিন্তু নমুনা ফেরত গ্রহণের জন্য মালিককে লিখিতভাবে জানানোর তারিখ হইতে এক মাসের মধ্যে তিনি উহা ফেরত নিতে ব্যর্থ হইলে কমিশনার অব কাস্টমস যেরূপ নির্দেশ করেন সেইরূপ প্রক্রিয়ায় উহার বিলিব্যবস্থা করা যাইবে।

(৪) পদমর্যাদায় সহকারী কমিশনার অব কাস্টমসের নিম্নে নহেন এইরূপ কাস্টমস কর্মকর্তা কর্তৃক নির্ধারিত শর্ত সাপেক্ষে, কোন আমদানিকৃত অথবা রপ্তানিযোগ্য পণ্যের মালিক অথবা তাহার নিকট হইতে ক্ষমতাপ্রাপ্ত প্রতিনিধি বিল অব এন্ট্রি অথবা, ক্ষেত্রমত, বিল অব এক্সপোর্ট উপস্থাপন অথবা প্রেরণ করার পূর্বে নমুনা উত্তোলন করিতে পারিবেন।

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer has the authority to take samples of goods for the purpose of examination, chemical analysis, or valuation at the time of entry, clearance, or while the goods are passing through a customs area.

The exchange rate is officially determined by the National Board of Revenue or an officer authorized by them.
The exchange rate is defined as the rate determined by the government for converting Bangladeshi currency into foreign currency or vice versa.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is empowered to determine the exchange rate and to specify, via gazette notification, the freight charges for goods transported by air that are delivered or potentially delivered to the buyer at a customs airport.
Foreign Currency Regulation Act 1947: The definitions of foreign currency and Bangladesh currency for the purposes of customs valuation are derived from the meanings assigned to them under this Act.
Customs Valuation: For valuation purposes, the cost of goods includes freight, insurance, commissions, and other incidental charges incurred for delivery to the place of importation or exportation.

Agent: An agent is defined as any person, such as a shipping, clearing, forwarding, or cargo agent, who is licensed under section 207 or permitted to transact business under section 208 of this Act.

Officer of Customs: An appropriate officer is defined as an officer of customs tasked with specific functions assigned by or under this Act. The term officer of customs generally refers to any individual appointed under section 3.
Bangladesh customs-waters: This defines the maritime jurisdiction of the Act as the sea area extending twelve nautical miles from the appropriate baseline on the Bangladesh coast.
Bill of Entry: A bill of entry is a document delivered under section 79, which now includes electronically transmitted versions containing particulars specified by the National Board of Revenue.
Bill of Export: A bill of export is a document delivered under section 131, which includes electronically transmitted versions containing particulars specified by the National Board of Revenue.
National Board of Revenue: The Board refers to the National Board of Revenue, which is the entity constituted under the National Board of Revenue Order 1972.
Coastal Goods: Coastal goods are defined as items transported by vessel between ports in Bangladesh, excluding any imported goods for which customs duty remains unpaid.
Container: A container is a durable, enclosed receptacle of at least one cubic meter, specifically designed for the repeated carriage of goods across multiple transport modes without intermediate reloading.
Controlling Authority: This refers to the owner, legal occupier, or any person holding legal control over a customs-airport, customs-port, customs-inland container depot, or customs-station.

Customs Airport: A customs-airport is any airport declared as such under section 9 of the Act.
Customs-area: A customs-area includes the limits of a customs-station as specified under section 10, encompassing locations where imported or export-bound goods are stored pending customs clearance.
Customs Computerised Entry Processing Sy: Defined as the Customs computer system, this is an automated processing system established by the National Board of Revenue to facilitate the purposes of this Act.
Customs-inland container depot: This is any location declared as a customs-inland container depot under section 9 of the Act.
Customs Port: A customs-port is any place declared under section 9 to be a port for the landing and shipment of goods.
Customs Station: A customs-station refers collectively to any customs-port, customs-airport, or land customs-station.
Export Manifest: An export manifest is a document delivered under section 53, including electronically transmitted versions containing particulars specified by the National Board of Revenue.
Goods: Goods are defined broadly to include all movable property, specifically including conveyances, stores, materials, baggage, currency, negotiable instruments, and electronic data.
Import Manifest: An import manifest is a document delivered under sections 43 and 44, including electronically transmitted versions containing particulars specified by the National Board of Revenue.
Land Customs Station: A land customs-station is any place, including inland river ports, declared as such under section 9.
Master of the Vessel: The master is the person, excluding pilots or harbour masters, who has command or charge of a vessel.
Person: For the purposes of this Act, a person includes companies, partnerships, associations, firms, or any body of persons.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: An entity appointed under section 25A to conduct pre-shipment inspections, including its representatives.
Prescribed: The term prescribed signifies that requirements or details are set out by rules or official orders made under this Act.
Registered User: A registered user is any individual or entity authorized and registered to access the Customs computer system for the purposes of the Act.
Rules: Rules refer to the regulations and operational procedures established under the authority of this Act.
Smuggling: Smuggling involves the illegal import or export of restricted goods, evasion of customs duties/taxes, or use of unauthorized routes, and includes any attempts, abetment, or concealment of such activities.
Special Bonded Warehouse: This is a private warehouse licensed under section 13 for hundred percent export-oriented industries, designated by the National Board of Revenue for specific exemptions.
Warehouse: A warehouse is defined as any place appointed under section 12 or licensed under section 13 of the Act.
Warehousing Station: A warehousing station is a location officially declared as such under section 11.
Wharf: A wharf is a place within a customs-port, approved under section 10(b), designated for the loading and unloading of goods.

When collecting samples, the officer must ensure the presence of the owner or their agent.
In the case of food or drug items, the officer may collect samples for examination by specified government or local authority officials if authorized by a general or special government order.
Agent: The agent of the owner of the goods is required to be present when samples are being drawn by the appropriate officer of customs.
Goods: Samples of goods may be drawn for testing, examination, or valuation during the customs clearance process or while within the customs-area.
Once the purpose for testing or examination is fulfilled, samples should be returned to the owner if it is practicable to do so.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to direct the disposal of samples if the owner fails to collect them within one month of receiving a written request to do so.
Government: The government may issue general or special orders authorizing the collection of samples for food or drug products to be examined by specific authorities.
Imported or Exported Goods: Owners or their authorized representatives may request to draw samples of goods prior to the formal submission of a bill of entry or bill of export, provided they meet the conditions specified by a customs officer at or above the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs.
Authorized Representative: An authorized representative is permitted to draw samples of goods before the formal filing of entry or export documents under specific conditions established by an Assistant Commissioner of Customs or a higher-ranking officer.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: An Assistant Commissioner of Customs or any officer of higher rank holds the authority to set the conditions under which an owner or authorized representative may draw samples of goods prior to the filing of a bill of entry or bill of export.
Bill of Entry: The owner or authorized representative may draw samples of imported goods before the presentation of the bill of entry, subject to compliance with conditions set by a senior customs officer.
Bill of Export: The owner or authorized representative may draw samples of export goods before the transmission of the bill of export, subject to compliance with conditions set by a senior customs officer.

Exporter: Exporters are required to submit information necessary for the proper valuation of goods intended for export and must produce relevant books and documents upon request.
Warehouse: The schedule covers matters pertaining to manufacturing and other operations conducted within a warehouse.
It authorizes the charging of expenses when a customs officer is specially employed to accompany an owner to the warehouse and fees for permitting owners to deal with goods therein.

It sets out conditions for granting port clearance to the master of a vessel, including requirements for security regarding the delivery of manifests.
Conveyance: The schedule provides for the sealing of conveyances carrying transit goods and general regulation of vessel departures.

Transshipment of Goods: The schedule governs the prohibition, regulation, and restriction of transshipment of goods without payment of duty.

Frustrated Cargo: The schedule provides for the regulation of the export of frustrated cargo in accordance with specific sections of the Act.
Transit and Transshipment: The schedule details conditions and restrictions for the transit of goods to foreign territories without payment of duty.

Bill of Export: The schedule explicitly includes the Bill of Export as a matter for regulatory provision.
Baggage: The schedule covers the definition, declaration, custody, examination, assessment, and clearance of passenger and crew baggage.
It regulates the transit and transshipment of baggage and defines the conditions under which baggage may be exempt from duty.
Coastal Goods: The schedule provides for the prevention of the illegal export of dutiable or prohibited coastal goods.
It includes measures to prevent the substitution of imported or export goods with coastal goods on board a vessel and regulates the conveyance of specific classes of goods between coastal ports.
Agent: The schedule mandates the licensing of agents, including the specification of fees, qualifications, and conditions of validity.
It provides for the imposition of penalties, suspension, or revocation of licenses and the right to appeal these administrative actions.

Customs Duty: Customs duty is levied on goods based on their value, which is determined according to the actual price paid or payable under fully competitive international trade conditions.
The Government may fix tariff values or minimum values for any goods chargeable with customs duty ad valorem, though if the declared value is higher, it serves as the basis for duty calculation.
Value: The value of goods for assessment purposes includes all costs such as freight, insurance, commissions, and other incidental charges related to sale and delivery at the place of importation or exportation.
Bill of Entry: The time of importation is defined as the date on which a bill of entry is delivered under the relevant legal provisions.
The bill of entry serves as the official document for determining the place and time of importation for valuation purposes.
Bill of Export: The time of exportation is determined by the delivery of a bill of export or, in cases where no such bill is required, the time when goods arrive at the customs port, airport, or station for export.
The place of exportation is the customs location where the bill of export is formally submitted.
Exchange Rate: The exchange rate for computing the value of goods is calculated based on the average rate prevailing during a specific thirty-day window prior to the submission of the bill of entry or bill of export.
The rate of exchange is fixed by the National Board of Revenue or an authorized officer, and is defined as the rate for converting Bangladesh currency to foreign currency or vice versa.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is empowered to fix the exchange rate for valuation purposes and to notify fixed freight charges for goods transported by aircraft to customs airports.
Foreign Currency Regulation Act 1947: This Act provides the legal definitions for foreign currency and Bangladesh currency as used in the context of customs valuation.
Government: The Government holds the authority to fix tariff values or minimum values for goods through official gazette notifications and to determine official exchange rates.

Drawback of the export on imported goods.- Subject to the subsequent provisions of this Chapter and the rules, when any goods, capable of being easily identified, which have been imported into 1[Bangladesh] and upon which customs-duties have been paid on importation, are exported to any place outside 1[Bangladesh] or as provisions or stores for use on board a conveyance proceeding to any foreign territory, 2[such duties, not exceeding seven-eights thereof] shall be repaid as drawback, subject to the following conditions, namely:-

Customs Duty Drawback: A portion of customs duties paid on imported goods may be repaid as a drawback when those goods are subsequently exported to a place outside Bangladesh.
The amount of the drawback repayment is limited to a maximum of seven-eighths of the duties originally paid upon importation.
Imported Goods: To qualify for a drawback, goods must be capable of being easily identified and must have had customs duties paid upon their original importation into Bangladesh.
Export: Goods qualify for drawback if they are exported to a foreign destination or are supplied as stores or provisions for a conveyance traveling to a foreign territory.
The exportation must occur within two years of the original importation date, though this period may be extended by authorized customs officials for sufficient cause.
The limit for any extension of the export deadline is set at three years from the date of the original importation.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer is tasked with verifying the identity of the goods to ensure they are the same items that were originally imported.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner has the authority to extend the two-year deadline for entering goods for export upon sufficient cause, provided the total time does not exceed three years.
Bill of Export: For the purposes of determining compliance with time limits, goods are considered to have been entered for export on the date the bill of export is delivered to the appropriate officer.
